query: Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in a simple solid-solution state has favorable plasticity and machinability but relatively low hardness and strength, while its deformation behavior remains poorly understood. Under mechanical-property and deformation testing, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs this low hardness and strength and why? Define a controlled comparison, predict the observations relative to the starting state, state the applicable composition, structural-state, and loading boundaries, connect the hypothesis to the reported property combination, and specify a falsification test.

cited_evidence.text: The tunable phase stability of these HEAs with varying Al concentrations () along with the nanolamellar structure () raise several interesting and yet important questions. What are the deformation mechanisms in the nanolamellar HEAs with alternating low and high Al concentrations? Are there differences in the phase stability and dislocation activity between low–Al concentration and high–Al concentration lamellae? What are the effects of lamella thickness and crystalline orientation on their deformation mechanisms and mechanical properties? What is their mechanical performance, as compared with homogeneous HEAs? Clearly, answers to these critical questions not only are of importance for the in-depth understanding of deformation mechanisms and mechanical properties of HEAs with nanolamellar structures but also provide useful guideline for their rational design. This is the motivation for the current study.

As shown in Fig. 1a, the DP-HEA displays a remarkable combination of strength and ductility with a tensile strength approaching 1 GPa and a tensile ductility of almost 60% at ambient temperatures, properties which are substantially higher than many single-phase HEAs, including the Cantor alloy. In order to discern the role of the constituent two phases and the salient deformation mechanisms, the DP-HEA was investigated using several nanoscale techniques, including in situ straining tests and quantitative in situ compression tests in the TEM, state-of-the-art spherical aberration-corrected scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) and energy-dispersive x-ray spectroscopy (EDS) with atomic resolution. Although deformation-induced phase transformations are known to occur in DP-HEAs, our current in situ TEM studies demonstrate that the phase transformation from fcc to hcp is based on the formation of three-dimensional (3D) stacking-fault networks comprising multiple stacking faults (SFs) and sessile Lomer–Cottrell locks, which we believe are promoted by intrinsic chemical variation in HEAs.
